nameStory: Staurastrum minnesotense gets its genus name from the Greek words 'stauros' meaning cross and 'astron' meaning star, referring to its distinctive star-like shape when viewed under a microscope. The species name 'minnesotense' honors Minnesota, where this tiny aquatic organism was first scientifically described and studied.
description: Staurastrum minnesotense is a microscopic single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. This tiny organism is invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 30-50 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). When viewed under a microscope, it has a beautiful star-like or cross-shaped appearance with radiating arms or projections. Like other green algae, it contains chlorophyll and can photosynthesize, contributing to the green tint you might notice in pond water.

idTips.label: Star-shaped form
idTips.description: Under magnification, the cell has a distinctive cross or star pattern with radiating arms extending outward from a central body

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Completely invisible to the naked eye - you'll need at least 100x magnification to see individual cells clearly

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: Bright green color due to chlorophyll, similar to the green you see in pond scum or algae blooms

idTips.label: Symmetrical structure
idTips.description: The cell shows perfect radial symmetry, like a tiny green snowflake or geometric crystal

idTips.label: Cell wall texture
idTips.description: The outer wall may appear smooth or slightly granular under high magnification, with distinct patterns unique to this species

habitat: Staurastrum minnesotense inhabits quiet freshwater environments including ponds, small lakes, marshes, and the slow-moving backwaters of streams throughout New England. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral water conditions and is often found in areas with organic matter like fallen leaves or decaying plant material. You're most likely to encounter it in shallow, sun-warmed waters where other green algae and aquatic plants are also thriving.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water temperatures warm and daylight hours lengthen, contributing to the early spring 'greening' of pond waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction. Water may appear notably green from algae blooms.
seasonality.fall: Numbers gradually decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases, though some individuals persist in warmer microhabitats.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or present in very low numbers, surviving as resistant cells until spring conditions return.

funFact: Despite being a single cell smaller than a pinhead, Staurastrum minnesotense is considered one of nature's most beautiful geometric forms - Victorian microscopists were so enchanted by these 'living crystals' that they created elaborate artistic arrangements of different species for display, treating them like tiny jewels from an invisible world.
confusionNotes: Staurastrum minnesotense can be confused with other star-shaped Staurastrum species, but each has unique arm shapes and proportions. Look for the specific pattern of projections and the overall size ratio between the central body and radiating arms - minnesotense tends to have more robust, evenly-spaced projections compared to its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: While called an 'alga,' Staurastrum belongs to a special group called desmids that are actually more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds. These organisms are considered living indicators of water quality - their presence often signals clean, unpolluted freshwater ecosystems.
compareHints: Staurastrum minnesotense differs from its many relatives in the genus by its specific arm configuration and proportions - while species like S. arctiscon has more delicate, needle-like projections, minnesotense shows broader, more substantial radiating structures. The central body is also typically more robust compared to species like S. longispinum, which has extremely elongated spines. Each Staurastrum species is like a different style of geometric art, with minnesotense representing a balanced, symmetrical design.
